1.1. WHAT IS AI?
So, what exactly is AI?

Is it the robots in "Ex Machina"? The all-knowing HAL 9000? Or maybe just your phone trying (and often failing) to autocorrect your texts? Let’s cut through the buzzwords and confusion to give you the full lowdown on artificial intelligence.
Artificial Intelligence, or AI, is the simulation of human intelligence in machines.

Basically, we’re trying to make computers think, learn, and problem- solve like humans. We want machines to work as well (or even better) as our brains do. Sounds wild, right? AI isn’t just about building robots that can outsmart us (although, yes, that’s a subplot in the sci-fi genre); it’s about designing systems that can handle specific tasks or even learn over time—a concept we’ll revisit in Chapter 4 called machine learning.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) refers to the development of systems or machines that can simulate or mimic human intelligence and behavior, allowing them to perform tasks such as learning, reasoning, and adapting autonomously.
However, the definition of "intelligence" itself is debated, as it can encompass a spectrum from imitating human-like reasoning to achieving ideal rational outcomes, which might not always align.
If you’re scrolling TikTok and someone says, “AI is the future,” it might feel like they’re just trying to sound deep. But let’s unpack what AI actually involves in three levels:
Narrow AI (ANI): Think of this as single-task AI. It’s designed to do one thing well—like Siri understanding your voice or Google Photos identifying your dog in every picture.

ANI is super common and already powering a lot of the tech you use daily. Some examples of ANI include Siri helping you set reminders, Google suggesting search results as you type, and your email inbox filtering out spam.

General AI (AGI): This is the holy grail—machines that can think and reason like humans. AGI could solve problems, understand emotions, and multitask like a pro. Spoiler alert: we’re not quite there yet, and experts debate if we’ll ever be.

Superintelligence (ASI): This is the realm of science fiction, where machines are way smarter than us. Think Skynet or Ultron—AI so powerful it could (potentially) take over the world. This is why some folks, like Elon Musk, are screaming, "Hey, maybe let’s not unleash a robo-apocalypse."

We explore these “levels” of AI deeper in section 1.3. Think of your favorite AI tool. Would you categorize it as ANI, AGI... or maybe, even ASI?
so, how does ai work?
AI isn’t magic; it’s math. (Sorry to burst your bubble.) At its core, AI relies on algorithms—step-by-step instructions—to process data and make decisions. Here’s the tea:
Rule-Based Systems

Old-school AI, or Good Ol' Fashioned AI (GOFAI hehe), focused solely on logic and pre-written rules. Imagine creating a flowchart with a billion "if this, then that" conditions. These systems could handle simple tasks like diagnosing car engine problems or playing tic-tac-toe, but they fell apart when things got unpredictable. Think of them as that super organized friend who has a meltdown when the Wi-Fi goes down.
Early chatbots like ELIZA, created in the 1960s, used rule-based responses to simulate conversations. It wasn’t "intelligent," but it fooled a lot of people into thinking it was.

Machine Learning

Fast forward to today, and we’re living in the age of machine learning (ML). ML flips the script—it doesn’t rely on hand-written rules but instead learns from data. Think of it like teaching a toddler: you show it thousands of pictures of cats, and over time, it figures out what a cat looks like. Sure, it might confuse a raccoon for a cat once in a while, but hey, we all make mistakes.
Machine learning uses datasets (big ones!) and algorithms to find patterns. For example, you give it a dataset of emails labeled "spam" or "not spam," and it learns to filter out spam on its own.
From recommending TikTok videos to predicting the weather, ML powers a lot of the tech you use daily.
Deep Learning

Deep learning (DL) takes machine learning to the next level. It uses neural networks, which are loosely inspired by how our brains work. Think layers of interconnected nodes—each "neuron" processes a piece of data, like recognizing edges in an image, and passes it along. By stacking these layers (hence "deep" learning), the system gets better at complex tasks.

Neural networks use layers of "neurons" to process data. The input layer takes in raw data (like pixels from an image), the hidden layers process and learn patterns, and the output layer delivers the result (like "this is a cat").

Deep learning has crushed it at tasks like translating languages, diagnosing diseases, and even beating human champions in games like chess and Go. We talk about AlphaGo in Section 1.2 - that’s a perfect example of Deep Learning flexing on us.

AI IS MORE THAN TECHNOLOGY

Some see AI as a mirror, reflecting our hopes and fears about what it means to be human. Others are like, “Can you guys chill? AI’s just here to optimize spreadsheets.” Both takes are valid, depending on your vibe.

1.2. a brief history of ai
The history of AI is one juicy glow-up story: humble beginnings, setbacks, breakthroughs, and finally, the main character moment we’re living in now. Let’s get into it!
1950s: The Birth of an Idea

Let’s kick things off with Alan Turing, the OG of artificial intelligence. In 1950, he wrote the iconic paper, "Computing Machinery and Intelligence," and asked the big question: "Can machines think?"
COMPUTING MACHINERY & INTELLIGENCE Alan turing

He proposed the Turing Test, a way to figure out if a machine could imitate human intelligence well enough to fool a person. Spoiler: this idea is still influencing AI today.
The Turing test involves a human evaluator who engages in natural language conversations with both a human and an AI participant, without knowing which is which.

If the evaluator cannot reliably distinguish between the human and AI responses, the machine is said to have passed the test. This approach helps measure AI's capability to demonstrate human-like intelligence in conversation.

In 1956, AI became official at the Dartmouth Summer Research Project where the term "artificial intelligence" was coined. Think of this conference as AI’s first big debut. It’s where legends like John McCarthy and Marvin Minsky got the ball rolling. (We stan Marvin Minsky!!)
1960s & 1970s: Things are happening, but...

The 1960s were all about rule-based systems. Researchers were building programs to solve algebra problems, recognize shapes, and even translate languages. But these early systems were super rigid. They could only handle tasks they were specifically programmed for (based on rigid rules).
Things started to slow down in the 1970s during what we now call the first AI Winter (brrr 🌬️). Funding dried up because people realized true AI was harder than it looked.
1980s: AI Returns with a Vibe Check
AI made a comeback in the 1980s with expert systems. These programs used rules and logic to make decisions.
At the same time, researchers started experimenting with neural networks inspired by how the human brain works. Neural networks would later become the backbone of modern AI.
1990s: AI Gets Competitive

The 1990s had LOTS of milestones. IBM’s Deep Blue defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, proving that machines could outsmart humans (at least on the chessboard). This was the moment AI started flexing on us.

And let’s not forget about speech recognition. In 1994, researchers achieved the first human-level spontaneous speech recognition system. Sphinx-II, a system designed by researchers at Carnegie Mellon University, used Hidden Markov Models to more accurately model speech using probabilities. This paved the way for virtual assistants like Siri and Alexa.

2000s: Data Takes Center Stage

Welcome to the era of Big Data. By the early 2000s, the internet was becoming a mainstream tool for communication, commerce, and entertainment. Devices like the iPhone (2007) made it easy for billions of people to access the internet, take photos, and use apps, generating data constantly. The cost of storing data also dropped significantly due to advances in hard drive technology and the rise of solid-state drives (SSDs).

Suddenly, researchers had access to massive datasets, which meant AI could start learning from lots of real- world information. This is when tools like Google Translate and early recommendation systems (hello, Netflix) started popping off.

The 2000s also gave us autonomous vehicles—shoutout to the DARPA Urban Challenge, a competition organized by the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency in 2007, where self-driving cars were tested IRL, with traffic laws and everything.
2010s: The Deep Learning Revolution
Here’s where AI really started serving looks. In 2012, Geoffrey Hinton’s team crushed the ImageNet competition using deep learning – machines could identify images better than ever before.
Google’s DeepMind made headlines in 2016 when its AlphaGo program defeated top Go player Lee Sedol. This was a big deal because Go is waaay more complex than chess.
And let’s not forget IBM Watson winning Jeopardy! in 2011, proving that AI could handle natural language and trivia like a boss.
2020s: AI in the Spotlight

Fast forward to now, and AI is everywhere. In 2020, OpenAI dropped GPT-3, a language model so powerful it could write essays, code, and even jokes (eh, kind of). Then came ChatGPT in 2022, which made conversational AI very mainstream. Your DMs will never be the same.

Think back to the Turing test we described on page 8. Do you think chatGPT would pass that test? What makes it successful or not successful?
AI is also making breakthroughs in healthcare (thanks, AlphaFold 2), autonomous driving, and creative fields like art and music. The possibilities are endless—and we’re just getting started.

The history of AI is filled with highs, lows, and breakthroughs that changed the game. From Turing’s question to the ChatGPT era, AI has come a long way—and you are about to learn how to be part of its future.
